claims.text: The initial Nb–Mo–Ta–W alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Slow furnace cooling after annealing at 1300°C for 1 hour promotes higher short-range chemical ordering.
Rapid quenching after annealing at 1300°C for 1 hour maintains a lower degree of short-range chemical ordering.
The extent of short-range chemical ordering can be quantified using advanced diffraction or atom-probe tomography.
Enhanced short-range chemical ordering increases local bond stiffness in Nb–Mo–Ta–W.
Enhanced short-range chemical ordering restricts dislocation mobility in Nb–Mo–Ta–W.
SRO-induced local bond stiffening produces a higher high-temperature elastic modulus.
Enhanced SRO alters the thermal-expansion behavior of Nb–Mo–Ta–W at high temperature.
Slow-cooled samples will have significantly higher elastic moduli than rapidly quenched samples between 1000°C and 1200°C.
Slow-cooled samples will have thermal-expansion coefficients different from those of rapidly quenched samples between 1000°C and 1200°C.
The rapidly quenched Nb–Mo–Ta–W sample has minimal SRO and represents standard solid-solution behavior.
Using comparable applied stress states makes SRO variation the primary cause of property differences between the cooling protocols.
Residual microstructural defects may influence the measured effect of SRO on thermoelastic properties.
